339 ``` 340 341 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 342 ::view-transition-group(site-header) { 343 animation: none; 344 z-index: 100; 345 } 346 ::view-transition-old(site-header) { 347 display: none; 348 } 349 ::view-transition-new(site-header) { 350 animation: none; 351 } 352 ``` 353 354 The `display: none` on the old snapshot prevents a flash where both old and new headers are briefly visible. The `name` prop gives the container an identity so React knows what to animate. The navigation triggers the transition; the `key={slug}` change makes React treat the old and new content as an exit/enter pair (activating `share`) instead of an in-place update. 422 423 If we click between photographer tabs, the grid crossfades. The tab bar and surrounding layout do not move. Only the photo grid transitions between states. 424 425 ## Next steps 426 427 You now know how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation. They need one fixed reference point to understand that the _content_ moved, not the entire viewport. 332 333 Assign the header a `viewTransitionName` and suppress its animation in CSS: 334 335 ```tsx filename="components/header.tsx" 336
337 {/* navigation links */} 338
339 ``` 340 341 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 342 ::view-transition-group(site-header) { 343 animation: none; 344 z-index: 100; 345 } 346 ::view-transition-old(site-header) { 347 display: none; 348 } 349 ::view-transition-new(site-header) { 350 animation: none; 351 } 352 ``` 353 354 The `display: none` on the old snapshot prevents a flash where both old and new headers are briefly visible. The `z-index: 100` ensures the header renders above the sliding content. 355 356 If we navigate forward to a photo, content slides left. If we click the "← Gallery" link (tagged with `nav-back`), content slides right. The header stays fixed throughout both transitions. 357 358 Browser-initiated back navigations (the back button or swipe gestures) do not carry a transition type, so the directional slide does not play. The shared element morph from Step 1 still applies if both pages have matching `name` props. 359 360 #### Keeping the page interactive 361 362 While a transition runs, the `::view-transition` overlay captures pointer events, so clicks during the animation are lost. Let them pass through to the live page: 363 364 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 365 ::view-transition { 366 pointer-events: none; 367 } 368 ``` 369 370 This restores interactivity for unnamed content. Hit-testing still skips named participants (like the anchored header) for the transition's duration, so keep transitions short and avoid naming elements the user clicks rapidly. 371 372 #### Respecting reduced motion 373 374 Directional slides simulate physical movement across the viewport. This is the most common trigger for motion sensitivity. Morphs, reveals, and crossfades carry less risk since they affect smaller areas or rely on opacity rather than position. 375 376 The simplest approach is to disable all animation durations: 377 378 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 379 @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { 380 ::view-transition-old(*), 381 ::view-transition-new(*), 382 ::view-transition-group(*) { 383 animation-duration: 0s !important; 384 animation-delay: 0s !important; 385 } 386 } 387 ``` 388 389 Without animation, content swaps instantly, which is the browser's default behavior. Each tab shows a different photographer's photos, but the route structure is the same: `/collection/[slug]`. Clicking between tabs does not feel like navigating to a new page. It feels like switching content within the same container. 394 395 A directional slide would be wrong here. Slides communicate "going to a new place." A crossfade communicates "same place, different content." The container persists (continuity), only the grid inside changes (swap). 396 397 Use a `ViewTransition` with `key` set to the current slug. events.content:
View transitions are in place and verified end-to-end in a headless Chromium against a production build: the thumbnail-to-hero morph, directional page slides, Suspense skeleton-to-content reveals, and reduced-motion handling all fire as intended.

## What changed

No new dependencies or config were needed. This Next.js 16.4 canary ships a React canary that exports `ViewTransition` from `react`, `@types/react` 19.3 already types it, and `<Link>` accepts a `transitionTypes` prop.

**`app/PageTransition.tsx` (new)** — a small wrapper around `<ViewTransition>` that maps the `nav-forward` / `nav-back` transition types to CSS classes and uses `default: 'none'` so untyped transitions (browser back button, refresh, Suspense reveals) don't slide. It wraps each page's content rather than the layout, because layouts persist across navigations and would never fire enter/exit.

**`app/ProductGrid.tsx`** — each thumbnail is wrapped in `<ViewTransition name="product-image-{slug}" share="morph" default="none">`, and each card's `<Link>` carries `transitionTypes={['nav-forward']}`.

**`app/product/[slug]/page.tsx`** — the hero gets the same `name` as its thumbnail so React pairs them and the browser morphs between them. The back link carries `nav-back`. The Suspense fallback is wrapped with `exit="slide-down"` and the async details with `enter="slide-up"`. I also changed the outer `<div>` to `<main>` so the detail page picks up the same max-width/padding as the grid page; the slide reads oddly if the two pages have different horizontal alignment.

**`app/page.tsx`** — same page wrapper and Suspense reveal treatment as the detail page.

**`app/globals.css`** — the animation definitions: a 400ms morph with a mid-flight blur to hide interpolation artifacts; asymmetric Suspense timing (150ms skeleton exit, then a delayed 210ms fade-in with a longer 400ms upward slide); ±60px horizontal slides for forward/back; `::view-transition { pointer-events: none }` so clicks aren't swallowed mid-animation; and a `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` block.

## Reduced motion

Rather than zeroing everything, the reduced-motion block removes all positional movement and blur but keeps short opacity fades, so state changes remain legible: page slides and Suspense reveals become plain crossfades, the morph snaps to its final position and crossfades in place, and the skeleton pulse becomes static.

One thing worth knowing about, since it's easy to get wrong: my first attempt used `animation: none` on the morph's `::view-transition-group`, which silently turned the morph into an instant swap. In Chromium the old/new snapshot pseudo-elements inherit `animation-duration` from the group, so the shorthand zeroed their crossfade too. Using `animation-name: none` instead keeps the crossfade; there's a comment in the CSS explaining this.

## Verification

Playwright drove a `next build` + `next start` instance, intercepting `document.startViewTransition` to record transition types, which elements carried a `view-transition-name` in the old and new DOM, and which keyframes ran on the `::view-transition-*` pseudo-elements. With motion enabled: forward navigation carried `nav-forward`, the clicked thumbnail and the destination hero shared the name `product-image-leather-backpack`, `via-blur` and `slide-x` ran, and the untyped Suspense reveal ran the `slide-y` exit and enter. With `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`: no `slide-x`, `slide-y`, or `via-blur` ran, only `fade-only` plus the browser's crossfade. A frozen mid-transition screenshot showed the thumbnail visibly in flight toward the hero slot. `tsc --noEmit` and `next build` both pass.

Two notes: the `package.json` and `package-lock.json` modifications in `git status` were already present before I started and aren't mine. And browser-initiated back navigation (the back button) carries no transition type, so it gets the morph but not the directional slide; that's inherent to the API, not something the app can tag.
